title: The Art of Serving and Decanting Old Wines
quiz.0.question: Before opening a Barolo stored lying down for 20 years, what is the most important first step?
quiz.0.options.0: Put it straight into the freezer to cool it quickly
quiz.0.options.1: Stand the bottle upright for at least 24-48 hours so the sediment settles to the bottom
quiz.0.options.2: Shake the bottle hard to wake up the sleeping aromas
quiz.0.options.3: Pull the cork out quickly with a corkscrew
quiz.0.explanation: Old wines contain a lot of sediment; if the bottle is not stood upright for it to settle, sediment will mix into the wine when pouring, bringing bitterness and spoiling the palate.
quiz.1.question: When opening an old wine, why is an "Ah-So (two-pronged) opener" recommended instead of a corkscrew?
quiz.1.options.1: Because old-wine openers also filter out sediment
quiz.1.options.2: Because old corks are usually very fragile and soggy, and a corkscrew easily breaks them into the wine
quiz.1.options.3: Because old-wine openers can inject oxygen at the same time
quiz.1.explanation: The Ah-So grips both sides of the cork with two thin metal blades and pulls it out intact, avoiding the risk of a corkscrew destroying the fragile cork.
quiz.2.question: Regarding "decanting" and "aeration" of old wine, which idea is correct?
quiz.2.options.0: Very old wines (30+ years) usually need to sit for hours in a wide-based decanter for full contact with oxygen
quiz.2.options.1: The main purpose of decanting is to expose the wine to lots of oxygen
quiz.2.options.2: For old wines with heavy sediment, choose a narrow-based, slender decanter to minimise the surface exposed to air and prevent over-oxidation
quiz.2.options.3: Young, tannic reds need no aeration and are best drunk straight away
quiz.2.explanation: Old wines are very fragile, and too much oxygen makes their aromas vanish quickly or even spoil. So decanting old wine is mainly about "separating the sediment", and a narrow-based decanter must be used to reduce oxidation.
quiz.3.question: Which glass shape is best for tasting aged Nebbiolo (such as old Barolo)?
quiz.3.options.0: A tall Champagne flute, to keep bubbles
quiz.3.options.1: A Burgundy glass with a wide bowl and inward-curving rim, to open up and concentrate complex tertiary aromas
quiz.3.options.2: A sweet-wine glass with a flared rim, to emphasise sweetness
quiz.3.explanation: Aged Nebbiolo has extremely complex aromas (such as rose, truffle and leather); a wide bowl gives room for them to evaporate, and the narrower rim concentrates these precious aromas towards the nose.
slides.0.title: The Art of Serving and Decanting Old Wines
slides.0.subtitle: Works of art made by time: how to protect and awaken great aged Italian wines
slides.1.title: The Two Challenges of Old Wine: Sediment and Oxidation
slides.1.content:
Top Italian reds aged more than 15-20 years (Barolo, Brunello, Amarone) are works of art made by time — the fruit has turned into complex tertiary aromas and the tannins are silky. But with that comes an extremely fragile wine that demands the most careful service.

🪨 Sediment

  • Anthocyanins and tannins bind and settle at the bottom of the bottle — a normal sign of ageing, not of a faulty wine
  • Harmless, but if mixed into the wine it brings bitterness and spoils the smooth texture
  • Solution: stand the bottle upright for 24-48 hours before opening so the sediment settles completely
  • When decanting, watch the sediment by candlelight/torchlight and stop pouring in time

💨 Oxidation risk

  • An old wine has already undergone long micro-oxygenation in the bottle and is extremely fragile
  • Sudden exposure to lots of oxygen (over-aeration) can make its complex aromas vanish within minutes
  • In severe cases it spoils rapidly: vinegar or soy-sauce notes appear, beyond rescue
  • Rule for wines over 30 years: decant only, do not aerate; pour into glasses straight after decanting and let the wine awaken slowly in the glass
slides.2.title: Preparing to Open: Four Key Steps
slides.2.content:
⏰ Stand upright for 24-48 hours

The most important first step — never skip it

An old wine stored lying down must stand upright for at least 24-48 hours before opening, so the fine sediment suspended in the wine settles fully to the bottom; the older the wine, the longer it needs — never rush to open it

🔧 The Ah-So old-wine opener

The saviour of fragile corks

Old corks are usually very fragile and soggy, and a corkscrew easily breaks them into the wine; the Ah-So (two-pronged) slides two thin metal blades into the gaps and grips the cork on both sides to pull it out intact, avoiding breakage

🕯️ Decanting by candlelight

A precise operation to separate the sediment

Under candlelight or a torch, pour the wine slowly and steadily into the decanter; as soon as the first trace of sediment approaches the neck, stop pouring at once; better to lose a little clear wine than let sediment in

🫙 Choose a narrow-based, slender decanter

Minimising the surface exposed to air

For decanting old wines choose a narrow-based, slender decanter (such as a duck decanter) rather than a wide-bottomed one, to minimise the surface of wine in contact with air and prevent over-oxidation from dissipating the aromas
slides.3.title: Decanting vs Aeration: Completely Different Purposes
slides.3.content:
"Decanting" and "aeration" are often confused, but they differ completely in purpose, the wines they suit and the tools used — distinguishing them correctly is core knowledge for handling old wine.

🫙 Decanting for Sediment

  • Purpose: separating the clear wine from the sediment at the bottom
  • For: old wines with heavy sediment (Barolo or Brunello over 20 years, vintage Port)
  • Decanter: narrow-based and slender (duck type), minimising contact with air
  • Timing: drink soon after decanting; for wines over 30 years pour into glasses immediately and let them awaken slowly in the glass
  • ⚠️ Key: decanting is for "removing sediment", not for exposing the wine to air

💨 Aeration for Breathing

  • Purpose: exposing the wine to oxygen to soften tannins, release aromas and remove reductive notes
  • For: young, tannic reds with closed aromas (young Brunello, Super Tuscans)
  • Decanter: wide-based (captain's decanter), maximising contact with air
  • Timing: leave for 1-3 hours (adjust to the wine and vintage)
  • ✅ Key: aeration is for "breathing", letting a young wine open up
slides.4.title: Glassware, Serving Temperature and Pace of Tasting
slides.4.content:
🍷 Choice of glass

The Burgundy glass

For aged Nebbiolo / Sangiovese choose a Burgundy glass with a wide bowl and an inward-curving rim; the wide bowl lets complex tertiary aromas (truffle, rose, leather) unfold fully, and the narrower rim concentrates these precious aromas towards the nose

🌡️ Serving temperature

16-18°C (slightly cooler than most reds)

Too warm makes the alcohol prickly and masks fragile aromas; slightly cooler keeps the wine tighter and livelier; take it out of the cellar (12-14°C) about 30 minutes before drinking and let it warm naturally at room temperature

👁️ Pace of tasting

Small pours, watching the whole evolution of the aromas

Pour a little at a time and don't rush to finish; follow the old wine's whole life cycle from closed (even reductive) on opening → gradually blossoming with flowers and truffle → aromas beginning to fade — this is the greatest pleasure of tasting old wine

⏳ The fragile window of old wine

Wines over 30 years may fade after 30-60 minutes

The complex aromas of very old wines may vanish within 30-60 minutes of opening; this does not mean the wine is faulty — the monument to time has completed its mission; have guests seated on time and don't let the old wine wait alone
slides.5.title: Key Takeaways
slides.5.points.0: The two challenges of old wine: sediment (bitterness) and oxidation risk (aromas dissipating), each needing a different strategy
slides.5.points.1: Step one: stand an old wine stored lying down upright for 24-48 hours before opening so the sediment settles fully
slides.5.points.2: Opening tool: the Ah-So (two-pronged) old-wine opener, avoiding a corkscrew breaking the fragile cork
slides.5.points.3: Decanting = separating sediment; aeration = exposing to oxygen to soften tannins — completely different purposes
slides.5.points.4: Decanting old wine: use candlelight and a narrow-based, slender decanter (duck type) to minimise contact with air
slides.5.points.5: Aerating young wine: use a wide-based decanter (captain's type) to maximise contact with air, for 1-3 hours
slides.5.points.6: Wines over 30 years: decant only, do not aerate — pour into glasses straight after decanting and let them awaken slowly in the glass
slides.5.points.7: Aged Nebbiolo/Sangiovese suits a Burgundy glass; serving temperature 16-18°C (slightly cooler than most reds)

slides.6.questions.4.question: When a sommelier helps a guest choose wine, what is the most effective opening question?
slides.6.questions.4.options.1: "What are you planning to eat tonight? Is it a special occasion?"
slides.6.questions.4.options.3: "Shall I recommend the most expensive red?"
slides.6.questions.4.explanation: The best consultative questions find out the "occasion + the food", so the most fitting pairing can be recommended, rather than starting from budget or brand preference. This also builds the guest's trust and improves the whole dining experience.
